title: A Still Small Voice
subtitle: 1 & 2 Kings in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin: The books of Kings begin with a young king asking for an understanding heart and end with an exiled king eating bread at a foreign table. In between: stones cut in silence at the quarry, a cloud of glory filling the temple, a cloak torn in twelve pieces, ravens at a brook, a widow's last handful of flour, fire on Carmel, a voice so quiet a prophet covered his face to hear it, a mantle dropped across a plowman's shoulders, a pot of oil that outlasted the jars, a river that made a proud captain clean, hills full of horses of fire, and a forgotten book found in the dust of the temple. This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts: Solomon and the temple, the kingdom torn in two, Elijah, Elisha, and the last kings to the fall of Jerusalem.

parts.title: A House for His Name
parts.epigraph: I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will not forsake my people Israel.
parts.lightHint: Where the luminous cloud of glory fills the quiet gold-and-cedar house

parts.title: A Lamp in Jerusalem
parts.epigraph: That David my servant may have a lamp always before me in Jerusalem.
parts.lightHint: Beside the torn cloak where one tribe is kept for David’s sake

parts.title: The God Who Answers
parts.epigraph: The God who answers by fire, let him be God.
parts.lightHint: At the mouth of the mountain cave where the still small voice speaks after the fire

parts.title: Open His Eyes
parts.epigraph: Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.
parts.lightName: Light of the Hills of Dothan
parts.lightHint: Along the ridge blazing with unseen horses and chariots of fire

parts.title: I Have Seen Your Tears
parts.epigraph: I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears.
parts.lightHint: Near the dial steps and the final table of daily bread before the Finale Plaza

paintings.title: the way of all the earth
paintings.epigraph: “I am going the way of all the earth. You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man”
paintings.poem:
an old king,
going the way of all the earth,
doesn't talk about swords
or borders.

he talks about walking.

keep his ways.
keep his word.
walk before him
with all your heart.

that's the strength
he means.

not the grip
of a hand on a throne,
but the steadiness
of feet on a path.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the way of all the earth” (1 Kings 2:1–3)—where the poem notes, “but the steadiness of feet on a path”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: an understanding heart
paintings.epigraph: “Give your servant therefore an understanding heart”
paintings.poem:
ask, God said,
and the whole night waited.

a young king
with everything to want
said,
I am just a little child.
I don't know how
to go out or come in.

then he asked,
not for long life,
not for riches,
but for a heart
that could hear.

and God was pleased.

sometimes the wisest thing
you can say
is how little you know,
and then ask
to be taught.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 1 Kings 3:5–10 (“and then ask to be taught”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: the living child
paintings.epigraph: “Give her the living child, and definitely do not kill him. She is his mother.”
paintings.poem:
two women,
one baby,
no witnesses.

the king didn't search
for evidence.
he searched
for love.

and he found it
in the one
who would rather lose her son
than see him hurt.

give her the child,
she said.
only let him live.

that was how he knew.

love will let go
before it lets
harm come.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the living child” (1 Kings 3:16–28)—where the poem notes, “before it lets harm come”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: cedar and hyssop
paintings.epigraph: “He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall”
paintings.poem:
the tall cedar of Lebanon
and the little hyssop
in a crack of the wall.

he had words for both.

wisdom notices
the small things too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “cedar and hyssop” (1 Kings 4:29–34)—where the poem notes, “wisdom notices the small things too”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: no hammer heard
paintings.epigraph: “The house, when it was under construction, was built of stone prepared at the quarry”
paintings.poem:
the stones were cut
somewhere else,
far off, at the quarry,
where the noise was.

by the time they reached the hill
they only had to be
set in place.

a house for God
rising
in silence.

maybe that's how he builds
in us too:
the hard shaping done
in places we'd rather forget,
so that when we arrive,
we fit.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “no hammer heard” (1 Kings 6:7)—where the poem notes, “so that when we arrive, we fit”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the cloud
paintings.epigraph: “the cloud filled Yahweh’s house, so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud”
paintings.poem:
the priests set the ark
in its place
and stepped out,

and a cloud came in
behind them
and filled the house,

so thick with glory
that no one
could stand to work.

all that cedar,
all that gold,
all that careful building,

and the best moment
was the one
when nobody could do
anything at all.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the cloud” (1 Kings 8:6–11)—where the poem notes, “when nobody could do anything at all”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: how much less this house
paintings.epigraph: “heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!”
paintings.poem:
he built the finest house
the land had ever seen,
then stood in front of it
with open hands
and said,
it can't hold you.

heaven can't hold you.

but hear us
when we pray toward this place.
and when you hear,
forgive.

not a house to keep God in.
a place to turn toward
when we need
to be found.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “how much less this house” (1 Kings 8:22–30) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: not even half
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, not even half was told me!”
paintings.poem:
she came a long way
with camels and spices and gold
and all her hardest questions.

she'd heard the stories.
she didn't believe them.

then she saw
the table,
the house,
the way up to the house of God,
and she had nothing left
to say.

not even half, she said at last.
not even half was told me.

some things you only know
by going to see.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not even half” (1 Kings 10:1–9)—where the poem notes, “some things you only know by going to see”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a little at a time
paintings.epigraph: “his heart was not perfect with Yahweh his God, as the heart of David his father was.”
paintings.poem:
it didn't happen in a day.

the man who asked for wisdom,
who prayed at the altar
with open hands,

grew old,
and his heart turned
a little,
and then a little more,

until there were altars
on the hill across the valley
to gods with other names.

nobody wakes up
far from God.

you drift
one small turn
at a time.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a little at a time” (1 Kings 11:1–8)—where the poem notes, “one small turn at a time”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: twelve pieces
paintings.epigraph: “Ahijah took the new garment that was on him, and tore it in twelve pieces.”
paintings.poem:
a prophet in a field
took off his new cloak
and tore it
into twelve pieces.

take ten, he told Jeroboam.
the kingdom would break.

but not all of it.
one tribe kept,
for David's sake,
for Jerusalem's sake,

so there would always be
a lamp.

even when God
lets things tear,
he leaves a light
burning.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “twelve pieces” (1 Kings 11:29–36) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: good words
paintings.epigraph: “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever.”
paintings.poem:
the old men said,
be their servant today
and they'll serve you forever.

the young men said,
make the yoke heavier.

he listened
to the young men.

and a kingdom
that had held together
through three kings
came apart
over one answer.

the gentle word
would have cost him
nothing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 1 Kings 12:1–16 (“would have cost him nothing”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: too far to go
paintings.epigraph: “It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem.”
paintings.poem:
it's too far, the king said.
too much for you.
stay here.
here is a god you can reach.

two gold calves,
one at each end of the land,
so no one would have
to make the climb.

it sounded like kindness.

but the easy road
led the people
away from the house
where God had put his name.

not every shortcut
is a mercy.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “too far to go” (1 Kings 12:26–30)—where the poem notes, “not every shortcut is a mercy”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the hand restored
paintings.epigraph: “pray for me, that my hand may be restored me again.”
paintings.poem:
the king stretched out his hand
to seize the man of God,
and it dried
and would not come back.

then the king said,
pray for me.

and the man he had just tried
to arrest
prayed,
and the hand came back
as it was before.

of all the signs that day,
maybe this was the clearest:
a prayer
for the one who was against him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where is God inviting you to set down your work today and rest in what He has already finished (1 Kings 13:1–6)?

paintings.title: ravens
paintings.epigraph: “The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.”
paintings.poem:
hide by the brook, God said.
the ravens will feed you.

of all the messengers,
birds that take,
not birds that give.

and yet:
bread in the morning,
bread in the evening,
and water running over stones.

he didn't get a storehouse.
he got a morning,
and then an evening,
and then another morning.

enough,
twice a day,
on black wings.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of 1 Kings 17:1–6?

paintings.title: a handful of flour
paintings.epigraph: “The jar of meal didn’t run out, and the jar of oil didn’t fail”
paintings.poem:
a widow gathering two sticks
at the city gate
for one last meal.

a handful of flour,
a little oil.
that was everything.

a stranger asked her
to make his bread first,
and she did.

and the next morning
there was flour in the jar,
and the next.

never full.
never empty.
just enough,
every time she reached in.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a handful of flour” (1 Kings 17:8–16)—where the poem notes, “just enough, every time she reached in”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: your son lives
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, your son lives.”
paintings.poem:
the boy stopped breathing,
and his mother
had only questions.

Elijah didn't argue.
he said, give me your son,
and carried him upstairs
and cried out to God.

three times he stretched out
over the child.

and God listened.

then down the stairs
with the boy in his arms:
see, your son lives.

some prayers
are carried up the stairs
in grief
and come back down
breathing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 1 Kings 17:17–24 (“and come back down breathing”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: how long
paintings.epigraph: “How long will you waver between the two sides?”
paintings.poem:
how long, he asked them,
will you stand there
between two roads?

and the people
didn't say a word.

silence
is an answer too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “how long” (1 Kings 18:20–21)—where the poem notes, “silence is an answer too”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: fire on Carmel
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh, he is God! Yahweh, he is God!”
paintings.poem:
all day they shouted,
and no one answered.

then Elijah rebuilt
the broken altar,
twelve stones,
one for each tribe,

and poured water on it
three times,
till the trench was full.

one short prayer
at the evening offering:
let them know
you have turned their hearts back.

and the fire fell
and licked up
even the water.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “fire on Carmel” (1 Kings 18:30–39)—where the poem notes, “and licked up even the water”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a cloud like a hand
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, is rising out of the sea.”
paintings.poem:
years without rain.

he bent down to the ground,
his face between his knees,
and sent his servant
to look at the sea.

nothing.
go again.
nothing.
go again.

seven times.

and then
a cloud no bigger
than a hand.

that was all he needed
to send word to the king:
hurry home,
before the rain.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a cloud like a hand” (1 Kings 18:41–45)—where the poem notes, “hurry home, before the rain”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: under the broom tree
paintings.epigraph: “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
paintings.poem:
after the fire,
he ran,
a day into the desert,
and lay down under a bush.
it is enough, he said.
take my life.

heaven didn't lecture him.
an angel touched him,
and there was bread
baking on the coals
and a jar of water.

eat, and sleep.
then eat again.
the journey is too much for you.

sometimes the holiest thing
is a warm loaf
and a little more sleep.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “under the broom tree” (1 Kings 19:3–8)—where the poem notes, “is a warm loaf and a little more sleep”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a still small voice
paintings.epigraph: “After the fire, there was a still small voice.”
paintings.poem:
a wind that broke the rocks.
not there.

an earthquake.
not there.

a fire.
not there either.

then something
so quiet
he had to cover his face
and step outside
to hear it.

what are you doing here, Elijah?

God doesn't always shout.
sometimes he asks
a gentle question,
and waits.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where is God inviting you to set down your work today and rest in what He has already finished (1 Kings 19:9–13)?

paintings.title: the mantle
paintings.epigraph: “Elijah went over to him, and put his mantle on him.”
paintings.poem:
a young man plowing
behind twelve yoke of oxen,
the last in the line.

a prophet crossed the field
and threw his cloak
across his shoulders.

that was the whole invitation.

and Elisha
boiled the oxen
over the wood of his own yoke,
fed the people,
and followed.

no plow left
to go back to.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “the mantle” (1 Kings 19:19–21) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: I will not leave you
paintings.epigraph: “Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.”
paintings.poem:
wait here, Elijah said.
at Gilgal. at Bethel. at Jericho.

I will not leave you,
Elisha said,
every time.

so they walked
and talked
all the way to the river,
and across it,

until fire came between them
and the old prophet
went up
in a whirlwind.

the last thing
they did together
was walk.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 2 Kings 2:1–11 (“they did together was walk”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: a double portion
paintings.epigraph: “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.”
paintings.poem:
ask, Elijah said,
before I am taken.

and Elisha
didn't ask for land,
or safety,
or a name.

he asked for more
of what he'd seen
in the man he'd followed.

that's a hard thing,
Elijah said.
if you see me go,
it will be yours.

so he kept his eyes on him
to the very end.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a double portion” (2 Kings 2:9–12)—where the poem notes, “so he kept his eyes on him to the very end”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: where is the God of Elijah
paintings.epigraph: “Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah?”
paintings.poem:
he picked up the cloak
that had fallen
and walked back to the river
alone.

the same water.
the same cloak.
no Elijah.

where is the God of Elijah?
he asked,
and struck the water.

and the river opened.

the prophet was gone.
God was not.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “where is the God of Elijah” (2 Kings 2:13–15) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: another jar
paintings.epigraph: “Bring me another container.”
paintings.poem:
a widow with debts,
two sons,
and one small pot of oil.

go borrow jars, Elisha said.
not just a few.

she shut the door
and poured,
and poured,
until her son said,
there isn't another one.

then it stopped.

the oil didn't run out.
the jars did.

bring more
than you think.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “another jar” (2 Kings 4:1–7)—where the poem notes, “bring more than you think”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a little room on the roof
paintings.epigraph: “Please let’s make a little room on the roof.”
paintings.poem:
a bed.
a table.
a chair.
a lamp.

that's all she gave him:
a small room on the roof
for a man who kept
passing by.

and when he asked
what he could do for her,
she said,
I live among my own people.

she wasn't trading.
she was only
making room.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a little room on the roof” (2 Kings 4:8–13)—where the poem notes, “she was only making room”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: it is well
paintings.epigraph: “It is well.”
paintings.poem:
the promised son,
grown into a boy,
died on her knees at noon.

she laid him on the prophet's bed,
shut the door,
and rode.

is it well? they asked.
it is well, she said,
and kept riding.

she caught hold of his feet.
I will not leave you, she said,
the words he once said
to his own master.

and in the little room on the roof
the child grew warm,
sneezed seven times,
and opened his eyes.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of 2 Kings 4:18–37?

paintings.title: the girl from Israel
paintings.epigraph: “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria!”
paintings.poem:
she was taken
from her home,
a little girl
serving in a foreign house.

she had every reason
to stay quiet.

but when she saw
the great captain's sickness,
she said,
I wish he could see the prophet.
he would heal him.

the whole story turns
on one small voice
that could have said nothing,
and didn't.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the girl from Israel” (2 Kings 5:1–4)—where the poem notes, “that could have said nothing, and didn't”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: wash, and be clean
paintings.epigraph: “his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.”
paintings.poem:
he came with horses and chariots,
silver and gold,
and the prophet
didn't even come to the door.

go wash in the Jordan.
seven times.

he was furious.
he had pictured something grand.

but his servants said,
if he'd asked some great thing,
wouldn't you have done it?

so he went down
into the plain little river.
once. twice.
seven times.

and came up
with the skin of a child.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “wash, and be clean” (2 Kings 5:9–15)—where the poem notes, “and came up with the skin of a child”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: it was borrowed
paintings.epigraph: “He cut down a stick, threw it in there, and made the iron float.”
paintings.poem:
it was borrowed,
he cried,
as the iron sank.

and God
lifted it from the river
for a man worried
about what he owed.

no loss
is too small
to bring him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “it was borrowed” (2 Kings 6:1–7)—where the poem notes, “is too small to bring him”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: more with us
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”
paintings.poem:
the servant got up early
and saw the army
all around the city.

what shall we do?

and Elisha didn't say
run,
or hide,
or it isn't as bad as it looks.

he prayed,
open his eyes.

and the hills
were full of horses
and chariots of fire.

the danger was real.
so was everything
he couldn't see.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “more with us” (2 Kings 6:15–17)—where the poem notes, “so was everything he couldn't see”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a day of good news
paintings.epigraph: “Today is a day of good news, and we keep silent.”
paintings.poem:
four lepers at the gate
of a starving city,
nothing left to lose,

walked into the enemy camp
at twilight
and found it empty.

tents. bread. silver.
they ate and drank.
they hid what they could.

then one of them said,
this isn't right.
today is a day of good news,
and we keep silent.

so the outsiders
went back to the city
that had shut them out
to tell it
there was bread.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a day of good news” (2 Kings 7:3–9)—where the poem notes, “to tell it there was bread”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: by every prophet
paintings.epigraph: “Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer”
paintings.poem:
turn back, he said,
by every prophet,
by every seer,
year after year.

Elijah on the mountain.
Elisha by the river.
voice after voice.

they would not listen.

and one day
the towers of Samaria
stood empty,
and the road east
was full of the people
who had lived there.

it wasn't that God
stopped speaking.

it was that no one
turned around.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 2 Kings 17:6–18 (“it was that no one turned around”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: spread before the Lord
paintings.epigraph: “Then Hezekiah went up to Yahweh’s house, and spread it before Yahweh.”
paintings.poem:
the letter was full of threats.
the empire at the door
had swallowed
nation after nation.

Hezekiah read it,
then carried it up
to the house of God
and spread it open.

here, Lord.
read this.
open your eyes and see.

you don't have to know
what to do
with the letter
in your hands.

you can lay it open
before him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “spread before the Lord” (2 Kings 19:14–19)—where the poem notes, “you can lay it open before him”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the shadow on the steps
paintings.epigraph: “Then he turned his face to the wall, and prayed to Yahweh”
paintings.poem:
set your house in order,
the prophet said.
you will die.

and the king
turned his face to the wall
and wept.

the prophet was not yet
out of the middle of the city
when God sent him back:

I have heard your prayer.
I have seen your tears.

and for a sign,
the shadow on the steps
went back ten steps.

no tear falls
anywhere
he isn't looking.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the shadow on the steps” (2 Kings 20:1–11)—where the poem notes, “anywhere he isn't looking”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: found in the house
paintings.epigraph: “I have found the book of the law in Yahweh’s house.”
paintings.poem:
they were only
fixing the building.

counting the money,
paying the masons,
buying timber and stone.

and somewhere in the dust
of God's own house
lay God's own word,
forgotten.

when they read it to the king
he tore his clothes.

not because the book was new.
because it was old,
and no one
had listened.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 2 Kings 22:3–11 (“and no one had listened”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: a tender heart
paintings.epigraph: “because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before Yahweh”
paintings.poem:
the word was hard.
the city would fall.
what was written
would come true.

but to the king,
this:

because your heart was tender,
because you wept,
I have heard you.

he couldn't change
what was coming.
he could still
be soft before God.

so he called everyone,
small and great,
up to the house of God
and read them every word.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a tender heart” (2 Kings 22:14–20)—where the poem notes, “up to the house of God and read them every word”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: bronze pomegranates
paintings.epigraph: “He burned Yahweh’s house, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem”
paintings.poem:
the house that was too small
to hold God
burned.

the cedar Solomon cut,
the stones shaped in silence,
the bronze pomegranates,
broken up and carried off.

the walls came down.
the people were led away.

and the heaviest thing
in the story
is not the fire.

it's how long
God kept calling
before it came.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “bronze pomegranates” (2 Kings 25:8–17)—where the poem notes, “God kept calling before it came”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: bread all his days
paintings.epigraph: “Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life”
paintings.poem:
thirty-seven years
a captive in Babylon.

then a new king
lifted his head,
spoke kindly to him,
changed his prison clothes,

and set bread before him
every day
for the rest of his life.

that's where the story ends.
not with the fire,
but with a son of David
at a table,
eating.

a lamp,
still burning
in a far country.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How has God quietly provided enough for today’s road, and who might you welcome to your table in kindness (2 Kings 25:27–30)?
